text.text: Two kinds of work run this company. Recurring services are the weekly and biweekly visits that fill each route day. pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A ten-minute tour of how the company's work flows through this workspace. Share it with the operations manager and every crew leader.
What lives where
Clients
: homes, HOAs, rentals and businesses, with turf area, gate notes, irrigation zones, what they owe, and what their recurring services are worth per visit.
Recurring services
: weekly and biweekly mowing and fertilizer programs, with route day, crew, price per visit and season dates.
Jobs
: one-off projects: cleanups, mulch, aeration, sod, planting, irrigation repairs.
Materials and equipment
: mulch, seed, irrigation parts, blades and oil, and what to reorder.
Invoices
: monthly mowing bills and project invoices.
How the week runs
Each route day, the crew works the stops on the Routes by day board.
Projects come in as
New request
; the office prices them, sets the crew leader and date, and moves them to
Scheduled
. A crew leader can press
Assign to me
Mark done
stamps the finish date. The office invoices the project that day and bills recurring services once a month.
Past-due invoices become
Overdue
; the client's Awaiting payment counts sent and overdue together.
Mark paid
stamps the date.
Your rhythm
Every morning: Dashboard, today's route, today's projects
Rain day: slide the routes and text the clients
Every Friday: count materials and equipment parts
Every month: send recurring bills, look at thin margins and weak route days
Making it yours

Rename crews and route days, add your own services and prices, and delete the sample clients once a dozen of your own are in. Type in any cell or drag cards between columns; every total updates by itself.
Billing recurring work
Bill weekly and biweekly clients once a month for the visits actually made. Count the visits from the route sheets, multiply by the
Price per visit

, and send one invoice per client. Skipped visits (drought, client request) are not billed; say so on the invoice so the client sees you are fair. Commercial clients often want a fixed monthly amount instead; agree it in writing and note it on their service.
Open jobs by crew, revenue by type of work and unpaid invoices.
Overdue jobs
My jobs
Overdue invoices
Awaiting payment (sent and overdue)
Route value by day
A route is profitable when the crew spends its day mowing, not driving. Group properties tightly, price by the visit, and protect the route day.
Build the route on a map first
List every recurring property with its
Turf area
from Clients.
Group them into tight clusters, one cluster per day. A crew of two to three can mow 14 to 20 average residential lawns a day, fewer when commercial lots are in the mix.
Set the
Route day
and
Crew
on each recurring service. The Routes by day board shows every day's stops at a glance.
Put the biggest commercial property early in the day, when the crew is fresh and before customers arrive.
Pricing a weekly visit
Start from minutes on site: mowing, trimming, edging and blowing, plus drive time to the next stop.
Multiply by your crew's loaded hourly cost and add your margin.
Steep banks, many beds, gates and dogs add minutes; write them in
Gate and access notes
so the price reflects them.
Every-other-week lawns grow longer between visits: price them at about 1.3 times a weekly visit, not half a month.
The Dashboard chart adds the per-visit value of each day. A weak day is the place to sell new stops.
Crew checklist at each stop
Gate closed behind you, pets checked
Pick up sticks and toys before mowing
Mow with sharp blades; alternate the stripe direction each week
Trim around beds, trees and fences; edge walks and drives every other visit
Blow clippings off hard surfaces, never into the street or storm drain
Note anything the client should know: irrigation leaks, sick shrubs, fence damage
Rain days
Do not skip a route day; slide it. Rain on Tuesday moves Tuesday to Wednesday and everything after it by a day. Saturday is the catch-up day. Text clients on the moved days.
Example

In spring the office notices that Friday carries only three stops worth under $350. They sell two nearby rental properties on every-other-week service and move the medical office from Thursday to Friday, which shortens Thursday's drive and fills Friday to the same value as the other days.
End of season
When the
Season ends
date nears, offer leaf removal and next year's fertilizer program to every recurring client. Mark services that stop as
Ended
rather than deleting them, so you can see who to call in the spring.
Spring cleanup sets the look of a property for the whole season, and it is where most new weekly clients are won. Price it fairly, do it in one visit, and sell the season while you are there.
Before the visit
Walk the property or use the client's photos. Count beds, measure linear feet of bed edge, and estimate the leaf and debris load.
Price by crew hours plus disposal, plus mulch or pine straw if the client wants it.
Book it as a project on the Jobs board with work type
Spring cleanup
and the
Crew size
On site
Remove leaves and winter debris from beds, under shrubs and along fences
Cut back ornamental grasses and perennials that were left standing
Prune winter damage; save shaping for after the first flush of growth
Re-cut bed edges with a half-moon or bed edger
Pre-emergent in beds where weeds were a problem last year
First mow of the season, a little higher than usual
Haul all debris; leave the property cleaner than the neighbors'
Mulch
Two inches is right; more smothers roots. Keep mulch off trunks and house siding.
One cubic yard covers about 100 to 160 square feet at two inches.
Hardwood mulch on most beds; pine straw where clients prefer it and on slopes.
Upsell, gently

The crew leader tells the office what they saw: thin turf (aeration in the fall), broken irrigation heads, overgrown shrubs. The office follows up with a price. Clients who have a cleanup are the easiest to sign for weekly mowing.
Example

A homeowner calls in March. The office measures 140 feet of bed edge from photos, prices a three-person crew for three hours plus nine yards of mulch, and books it. During the visit the crew leader notes two dead rotor heads; the office books an irrigation repair the next week and signs the client for weekly mowing starting in April.
Close-out
Enter real hours and material costs on the job, press
Mark done
, and send the invoice the same day. If the margin shows Thin, look at the hours first: cleanups usually run over because the debris load was underestimated.
Mulch, seed and fertilizer are bought in bulk and used in waves. Order too late and crews stand around; order too much and money sits in a pile behind the shop.
What to keep and how much
Mulch and pine straw
: in spring, a week's projects plus a buffer. Bulk mulch is cheaper by the truckload; bags only for small jobs.
Seed and starter fertilizer
: order in late summer for fall aeration season, based on the turf area of the clients who signed up.
Irrigation parts
: rotor and spray heads, nozzles, swing pipe, and a couple of valves in the sizes your clients use.
Equipment parts
: blades, trimmer line, belts, filters and two-stroke oil. A mower down for a day costs more than a shelf of blades.
The weekly count
Every Friday the operations manager counts the yard and the shop.
Type the count into
On hand
and set
Last counted
Anything showing
Reorder
goes on Monday's order. Bulk mulch is ordered by Wednesday for the next week.
Working out quantities
Mulch at 2 inches: square feet of bed divided by 160 gives cubic yards; round up.
Overseeding tall fescue: about 5 to 8 pounds per 1,000 square feet. Use the client's
Turf area
Pine straw: one bale covers about 50 square feet.
Checklist before a big project
Material on site or ordered with a delivery date
Dump trailer booked if hauling
Right blades and spare belts on the truck
Irrigation flags and paint if you will dig near lines
Example

In August the office adds up the turf area of 22 clients who booked aeration: about 190,000 square feet. At 6 pounds per thousand, that is roughly 1,140 pounds of seed, so they order 24 bags of 50 pounds plus starter fertilizer, before the supplier's fall price increase.
